body: Norway is a very mountainous country with many fjords along the coast, distinguishing it from the flatter landscapes of Denmark and Finland.
Most Norwegian houses are made of wood, often painted red or, more distinctively, black. Compared to Sweden and Finland, Norway has a higher percentage of wooden houses, even in suburban areas.
Norway uses standard long white European licence plates. A strong indicator for Norway is the presence of green licence plates, which are used for commercial vehicles.
Norwegian roads often have yellow middle lines with an orange tint and long dashed white outer lines on smaller roads. This combination helps distinguish them from Swedish and Finnish roads.
Norwegian road lines are often composed of small dots of paint.

The Norwegian language uses the unique letters Æ, Ø, and Å. The presence of Ø is a strong clue for Norway or Denmark, while the combination with frequent "kk" instead of "ck" points towards Norway over Sweden.
Norwegian bollards are thin and rectangular, distinguished by a reflector set inside a black parallelogram.
Norwegian snow poles are typically orange with a thin white reflector positioned towards the middle. This placement helps distinguish them from Swedish and Finnish snow poles.
Thin wooden snow poles with painted reflectors are a good indicator for Norway.
Guardrails supported by wooden posts are common in Norway, unlike in Sweden or Finland.
Norwegian pedestrian signs usually have four stripes with a simply drawn person. A version with a person wearing a hat is unique to Norway.
Norwegian directional signs are yellow with a black border. Road numbers appear in a green box for major roads or a white box for smaller roads.
Blue signs with a large white 'M' for meeting point are common on smaller roads. The Norwegian 'M' has a middle point that extends to the bottom, distinguishing it from the Swedish version.
A small, blue square sign with a white bus icon is the standard for Norwegian bus stops.
White signs with the text "Sone" are used to indicate zones, typically for speed limits, in urban areas.
Common Norwegian street suffixes are -veien and -gata or -gate, which are attached to the name.
Norwegian street signs are usually centered on top of their posts, unlike in Sweden where they are attached to the side.
Norwegian traffic signs have a white background, which is a key differentiator from the yellow backgrounds used in Sweden and Finland.
Road construction signs in Norway have a bright yellow background.
Smaller Norwegian road signs are often attached with four visible bolts in a tall rectangular pattern.
Norway uses yellow on black chevrons.
Small, white square kilometre markers show the road number, preceded by an 'R' or an 'F', and the distance. 'F' roads are county roads (Fylkesvei), often appearing as 'Fv' on maps.
Norwegian utility poles are typically wooden and may have a small black metal cap, a feature shared with Sweden and Finland.
Street lamps on wooden poles in Norway are mounted with a thick single bolt, unlike the double bolting used in Sweden and Finland.
Traditional Norwegian houses often feature grass-covered roofs, which is a strong clue for the country.
Norway has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, recognizable by its lower position and large, sometimes transparent, circular blur with a small protrusion.
The first digit of Norwegian road numbers generally indicates the region, helping with location identification. This pattern has exceptions, especially for 'Fv' (county) roads.
In northern Norway, you can find bilingual signs in Norwegian and Sámi. The Sámi language is recognizable by unique letters like Á and Đ.
The presence of bracken ferns, with their tall stems and wide leaves, is a good indicator for the south of Norway.
Spruce trees are primarily found in the southern half of Norway, especially the southeast and around Trondheim.
Pine trees are most common in coastal and far inland areas in the southern half of Norway.
Oak trees are predominantly found in the far south of Norway.
Maple trees are mainly found in the south of Norway, especially in the farmlands around Oslo.
Brightly coloured moss is a regional clue for the area between Lillehammer and Oppdal.
Large areas of farmland in Norway are concentrated in three main regions: the southeast, around Trondheim, and south of Stavanger.
The farmland in the southeast, near Oslo, is characterized by a flatter, rolling landscape with smooth, distant forested hills.
The farmlands around Trondheim are much hillier, with steeper and more uneven hills compared to the southeast.
The farmland south of Stavanger is flat and open, distinguished by vast grassy fields and rock walls made of large, round stones.
Deep fjords surrounded by tall mountains are most characteristic of the coastal region between Bergen and Trondheim.
The Lofoten archipelago is recognizable by its distinct, sharp, rocky mountains with minimal tree cover.
Northeast Norway features a rolling landscape with mainly very small birches and patches of grass instead of tall mountains.
Barren highlands with no trees or bushes, often featuring rocky mountains along the road, are predominantly found in southwest Norway.
Exposed rocky coasts with small coastal pines and bushes are typical along Norway's south coast.
The far north coastal roads feature grasslands with sparse vegetation and low, distant mountains.
Completely white wooden houses are common nationwide, especially in southern coastal villages.
Black snow poles are mostly found between Bergen and Trondheim.
Southeastern Norway features small wide black pole plates with single lines of letters and digits.
Rusty guardrails are almost exclusive to coastal regions, particularly the southern half of the west coast.
Svalbard is a separate unincorporated archipelago within Norway; a dedicated guide exists.
Large black or red pole plates are seen in Oslo.
Two red stripes around lampposts are common in Stavanger.
Bergen has a specific design of green fire hydrants.
The Russian border area features humid, green roads with overcast or foggy coverage, and low thin birch and pine trees.
Russian language occasionally appears on signs near the border along E6 and E105 near Kirkenes.
Røros is notable for its densely built traditional wooden architecture.
